text.tspan: Section 3.2: Measures of Variation
Although the centers are the same for each group, the dots are dispersed differently. The range for
the morning group is Range = 95 – 70 = 25. That means that all scores from the morning class fit
into an interval that is 25 points wide.
The range for the evening group is Range = 92 – 72 = 20. That means that the evening student
scores fit into an interval with width 20 points. Their scores are “closer together” and have less
variation in that sense. But there is more to the story! The morning group had one score in the 70’s,
three in the 80’s, and one in the 90’s. The evening group had two scores in the 70’s, only one in the
80’s, and two in the 90’s.
The morning group seems more consistent, even though they had the larger range. They had three
students score within 3 points of each other, 80, 82, and 83, and each of these was within 2 points of
the mean. That seems to be very consistent. So, in this example, the morning group, with the larger
range, seems like it has less variation. That is not the way we want a measure of variation to work.
For this reason, range is not the preferred way to describe variability.
We need a method to measure variation that considers more than just the highest and lowest values in the
data. How the data
in the middle
are spread out should count too. The next example further illustrates
how knowing the center and the range is not adequate in describing variation.

groups are populations. Find the mean, median, and range of each group, and make dot plots. Compare the
statistics. Do these statistics describe the data well?
